newsitem.title: USA: Storm kills one, causes New England floods.
newsitem.headline: Storm kills one, causes New England floods.

text.p: A vicious storm blamed for the death of a child continued to pound New England on Sunday, leaving thousands without power, flooding roads and homes and tearing boats from their moorings.

The National Weather Service reported overnight wind gusts of 81 mph (130 kph) in Little Compton, R.I. and winds of up to 70 mph (118 kph) accompanying the rain were expected to continue to plague much of New England throughout Sunday.
A 12-year-old boy in Babylon, N.Y., on Long Island was killed on Saturday when a tree uprooted by strong winds toppled onto him as the storm swept through the New York area.
The Weather Service issued a flood warning for north central Connecticut, where more than three inches (7.6 cm) of rain had fallen by early Sunday across Hartford and Tolland counties.
A flood watch was also in effect for all of Rhode Island, Massachusetts, and southern New Hampshire, as four to six inches of rain (10-15 cm) were expected on Sunday.
"This will certainly cause considerable street flooding and flooding in poor drainage areas as storm drains become clogged with leaves," the agency said.
The severe weather caused officials to cancel at least the morning heats at Boston's Head of the Charles rowing competition. It was the first time in the race's 33 years that events were cancelled.

The region's utilities, Boston Edison, Commonwealth Electric and Eastern Utilities, all reported scattered power cuts with no more than 2,000 customers in each of their service areas covering Rhode Island and Massachusetts being affected.

Connecticut residents were not so lucky and about 56,000 customers were without power there. In New York and New Jersey, many of the 100,000 customers who lost power on Saturday continued to experience scattered outages.
The Coast Guard in Boston said a number of small sailboats had been torn from their moorings during the storm.

The National Weather Service expected four to six inches (10 to 15 cm) of rain, with up to seven inches (17 cm) in some areas, in total to fall in New England before the storm was through. Heavy rains and high winds were expected to continue through the evening hours along the coasts of Massachusetts, New Hampshire and Maine.

The slow-moving storm on Saturday had dumped more than eight inches (20 cm) of rain in portions of the New York City-New Jersey metropolitan area, forcing the opening game of the World Series at Yankee Stadium to be delayed until Sunday.

The rain left 4.22 inches (10.7 cm) in Central Park. LaGuardia Airport got just over four inches (10.1 cm) of rain and Gillette, N.J., got 8.63 inches (21.9 cm) in one day, the National Weather Service said.
The storm, which moved slowly up the Eastern Seaboard, had flooded rivers and creeks from Philadelphia to Newark, N.J., but authorities said flood waters had receded by Sunday.
A flood watch remained in effect along the Rancoca Creek in Burlington County, N.J. Elsewhere, the alerts were downgraded to warnings.
